lesson.title: Mapping a Circuit by Its Voltages: The Node Voltage Method
lesson.summary: The node voltage method picks one reference node as ground and writes a KCL equation at every other node, turning a circuit into a small system of equations in the unknown node voltages.
lesson.body:
Every circuit has one node, and only one, worth singling out for special treatment: the reference node, often called ground, which we simply define to be at 0 volts. Once that choice is made, every other node's voltage is understood to mean the voltage difference between that node and the reference. The node voltage method uses this idea, combined with Kirchhoff's Current Law and Ohm's law, to reduce a whole circuit down to one unknown per node instead of one unknown per branch, which is usually a huge simplification.

The procedure is mechanical once you see it: choose a reference node and label it 0 volts, name the unknown voltage at every other node, then write one KCL equation per non-reference node, stating that the currents leaving that node sum to zero. Because the current through a resistor connecting node A to node B is simply (VA minus VB) divided by the resistance, by Ohm's law, every term in every equation can be written directly in terms of the unknown node voltages. Kirchhoff's Voltage Law is quietly built into this too, since the resistor current formula already assumes the voltage across the resistor is exactly the difference of the two node voltages, which is itself a KVL statement about the loop formed by the resistor and the two nodes.

Here is a concrete example. Node A connects to ground through a 4 ohm resistor and to node B through a 2 ohm resistor. Node B connects to ground through a 4 ohm resistor. A 6 amp current source injects current into node A. Writing KCL at node A: 6 equals VA divided by 4, plus (VA minus VB) divided by 2. At node B, with no source attached directly, the current arriving from node A must equal the current leaving to ground: (VA minus VB) divided by 2 equals VB divided by 4. Solving the second equation gives 2 times (VA minus VB) equals VB, so 2VA equals 3VB, or VB equals two thirds of VA.

Substituting into the first equation, VA minus VB becomes one third of VA, so 6 equals VA over 4 plus VA over 6. Using a common denominator of 12, that is 3VA over 12 plus 2VA over 12, or 5VA over 12. So VA equals 6 times 12 divided by 5, which is 14.4 volts, and VB equals two thirds of that, 9.6 volts. Checking node A: 14.4 divided by 4 is 3.6 amps, and (14.4 minus 9.6) divided by 2 is 2.4 amps, and 3.6 plus 2.4 is exactly 6 amps, matching the source. Checking node B: (14.4 minus 9.6) divided by 2 is 2.4 amps in, and 9.6 divided by 4 is 2.4 amps out, so the node balances perfectly.

This method scales to circuits with any number of nodes, and it is usually the fastest hand technique when a circuit has more nodes than independent loops. The one complication, what happens when a voltage source sits directly between two non-reference nodes so you cannot write a simple resistor current for that branch, is exactly the problem the supernode technique, covered next, is built to solve.
